---
title: "Single-Cell Embeddings"
---

A single cell is not one biological object but a snapshot of thousands of
transcripts at a moment in time. Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) turns
that snapshot into a vector of gene counts, and the embedding problem is to map
those sparse, noisy, high-dimensional vectors into a low-dimensional space in
which proximity means biological similarity. This chapter covers the data, the
classical pipelines, the probabilistic latent-variable models that dominate the
field, the recent cell "foundation models", and how integration is measured.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
A **cell embedding** is a mapping $\mathbf{z} = f(\mathbf{x})$ from a cell's
expression profile $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{g}$ over $g$ genes to a
low-dimensional vector $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$ ($d \ll g$), such that
distances in $\mathbf{z}$-space approximate biological relationships — cell type,
state, developmental trajectory — rather than technical covariates such as
sequencing depth or batch. Vector and matrix notation follows Appendix A:
$\mathbf{x},\mathbf{z}$ are column vectors, and a data matrix with $n$ cells is
bold uppercase, $\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times g}$.
:::

# The Data: Counts, Sparsity, and Technical Noise

## Count matrices

Droplet-based protocols such as the 10x Chromium system [@zheng2017massively]
barcode transcripts per cell, yielding a count matrix
$\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{N}^{n \times g}$ with $n$ cells and $g$ genes, where the
scalar entry $X_{ij}$ is the number of reads assigned to gene $j$ in cell $i$.
The matrix is stored as a sparse representation because the
overwhelming majority of entries are zero. Two properties of this matrix drive
most modeling choices:

- **Sparsity and "dropout".** A zero can mean the transcript is genuinely
  absent, or that it was present but not captured. This ambiguity is the
  single-cell analogue of missing data and motivates probabilistic models that
  treat zeros as observations rather than truth.
- **Library size.** Cells have different total counts
  $s_i = \sum_{j=1}^{g} X_{ij}$, reflecting differences in capture efficiency, not
  biology. Library size is the dominant technical covariate and must be modeled
  or normalized — see @eq-ch08-normalize.

Two further artifacts are endemic. **Doublets** are droplets that captured two
cells; their profiles look like an interpolated cell type and can seed spurious
clusters. **Cell-cycle phase** is a strong continuous covariate that separates
cycling and quiescent cells irrespective of identity. Neither is a biological
signal of interest for most tasks, and both must be regressed out or modeled.

::: {.callout-note}
## Definition
A **batch effect** is systematic technical variation between groups of cells
processed separately — different days, donors, chemistries, or sequencing runs —
that is confounded with the biological signal of interest. Integration methods
aim to remove batch variation while preserving biological variation.
:::

## Why the raw counts are a poor embedding

Using raw counts directly as features is unhelpful: the geometry is dominated by
sequencing depth, the axes are individual genes rather than interpretable
factors, and distances between cells correlate with technical rather than
biological state. Every downstream method in this chapter exists to replace raw
counts with a representation in which this is no longer true.

# Classical Pipelines: From Counts to a Neighborhood Graph

The standard Scanpy/Seurat workflow [@wolf2018scanpy; @hao2021integrated]
converts counts into a graph over cells through a fixed sequence of steps.

## Normalization and feature selection

Raw counts vary with sequencing depth before they vary with biology. Writing
$\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{N}^{n\times g}$ for the count matrix, the **library size**
of cell $i$ is $s_i=\sum_{j=1}^{g}X_{ij}$, and the standard pipeline rescales each
cell to a common target $s^{\ast}$ (Scanpy uses $s^{\ast}=10^{4}$) and then applies
the shifted logarithm,
$$
\tilde{X}_{ij}=\log\!\left(1+\frac{X_{ij}}{s_i}\,s^{\ast}\right),
\qquad \tilde{\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times g},
$$ {#eq-ch08-normalize}
a construction shared by Scanpy and Seurat [@wolf2018scanpy; @stuart2019comprehensive].

The logarithm is not cosmetic but a variance-stabilizing transform. If $X_{ij}$
follows a negative binomial with mean $\mu_{ij}$ and gene-specific
over-dispersion (concentration) $\theta_j>0$, then
$\operatorname{Var}[X_{ij}]=\mu_{ij}+\mu_{ij}^{2}/\theta_j$. By the delta method a
transform $f$ has variance
$\operatorname{Var}[f(X_{ij})]\approx[f'(\mu_{ij})]^{2}\operatorname{Var}[X_{ij}]$;
requiring this to be constant as $\mu_{ij}$ grows forces
$f'(\mu)\propto(\mu+\mu^{2}/\theta)^{-1/2}\to 1/\mu$, whose solution is
$f=\log$. Hence log-scaling tames the mean–variance relationship that would
otherwise let a few high-expression genes dominate Euclidean distances; the shift
$1+\cdot$ keeps the map finite at zero, where the count can legitimately be $0$.

After normalization the genes are filtered to a subset
$\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{1,\dots,g\}$ of **highly variable genes** (HVGs): the genes
whose observed spread exceeds the spread expected from technical noise at their
expression level. Following the Seurat convention [@stuart2019comprehensive], gene
$j$ is summarized by its dispersion $\delta_j=\log(\sigma_j^{2}/\bar{\mu}_j)$ and by
the within-bin standardized score
$$
Z_j=\frac{\delta_j-\bar{\delta}_{\operatorname{bin}(j)}}{\operatorname{sd}\!\big(\delta_{\operatorname{bin}(j)}\big)},
\qquad
\mathcal{H}=\big\{\,j \;:\; Z_j\ge\zeta \ \text{or } j \text{ among the } n_{\mathrm{HVG}} \text{ largest } Z_j\big\},
$$ {#eq-ch08-hvg}
where $\bar{\mu}_j=\frac1n\sum_i\tilde{X}_{ij}$ and
$\sigma_j^{2}=\frac1n\sum_i(\tilde{X}_{ij}-\bar{\mu}_j)^{2}$ are the gene mean
and variance, $\operatorname{bin}(j)$ is the expression bin containing gene $j$, and
$\bar{\delta}_{b}$ and $\operatorname{sd}(\delta_b)$ are the mean and standard deviation of
dispersion within bin $b$. Subtracting $\bar{\delta}_{\operatorname{bin}(j)}$ removes the mean–variance
dependence, so @eq-ch08-hvg selects genes with excess biological variability
rather than genes that are merely highly expressed; the threshold $\zeta$ and the
count $n_{\mathrm{HVG}}$ are user choices.

## Linear compression with PCA

Let $\tilde{\mathbf{X}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times g}$ collect the normalized,
HVG-restricted profiles and
$\boldsymbol{\mu}=\frac1n\tilde{\mathbf{X}}^{\top}\mathbf{1}_n\in\mathbb{R}^{g}$ be
the column means, where $\mathbf{1}_n$ is the all-ones vector of length $n$, so
that $\mathbf{X}_c=\tilde{\mathbf{X}}-\mathbf{1}_n\boldsymbol{\mu}^{\top}$ is the
**centered** matrix. Principal component analysis [@pearson1901lines] takes the
eigen-decomposition of the sample covariance,
$$
\boldsymbol{\Sigma}
=\frac1n\mathbf{X}_c^{\top}\mathbf{X}_c
=\mathbf{V}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{V}^{\top},
\qquad
\boldsymbol{\Lambda}=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_g\ge0),
$$ {#eq-ch08-covariance}
and projects the data onto the top $d$ eigenvectors,
$\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{X}_c\mathbf{V}_d\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$ with
$\mathbf{V}_d=[\mathbf{v}_1,\dots,\mathbf{v}_d]$. @eq-ch08-covariance is the
same construction as the truncated SVD of Appendix A applied to centered data: the
leading eigenvectors are the rank-$d$ linear approximation that minimizes
$\lVert\mathbf{X}_c-\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{V}_d^{\top}\rVert_F^{2}$, by the Eckart–Young
theorem. PCA is linear but effective: the leading components usually capture
library size, cell cycle, and the major cell-type axes, and $d$ is chosen where
the explained-variance ratio
$\sum_{k=1}^{d}\lambda_k/\sum_{k=1}^{g}\lambda_k$ flattens.

## Neighborhood graphs and visualization

Cells are connected into a $k$-nearest-neighbor graph in PCA space; this graph
is the workhorse structure for clustering (Leiden/Louvain) and for the
nonlinear visualizations UMAP [@mcinnes2018umap] and t-SNE
[@vandermaaten2008visualizing]. Both of these are for *visualization*: they
optimize local neighborhoods, not global geometry, and coordinates carry no
metric meaning.

## Clustering and annotation

Clustering operates on the neighbor graph rather than on the embedding
coordinates, so the graph is the actual object of interest for many downstream
analyses. Leiden communities are treated as candidate cell types, then annotated
by differential expression against marker genes and, increasingly, by
reference-based label transfer. The order matters: batch integration must happen
*before* clustering, because a graph built on unintegrated data will split each
cell type by batch.

```python
import scanpy as sc
adata = sc.read_h5ad("pbmc.h5ad")
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(adata, n_top_genes=2000)
sc.pp.scale(adata)
sc.tl.pca(adata, n_comps=50)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=15, n_pcs=30)
sc.tl.umap(adata)
sc.tl.leiden(adata)
```

This classical pipeline is fast, interpretable, and still the default baseline.
Its weakness is batch integration: PCA on concatenated batches separates batches,
and no step above is probabilistic about *why* a cell looks the way it does.

# Probabilistic Latent-Variable Models

The breakthrough that made batch-aware embeddings routine was to model each
cell's counts with a generative process and infer a latent vector.

## scVI

scVI [@lopez2018deep] models each count as a **zero-inflated negative binomial**
(ZINB) draw. For cell $i$ let $\mathbf{z}_i\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ be its latent vector,
$s_i=\sum_{j}X_{ij}$ its library size, and $\mathbf{b}_i$ a one-hot batch
covariate. Given $(\mathbf{z}_i,\mathbf{b}_i)$ the decoder with parameters
$\theta$ produces, per gene $j$, a normalized mean $\rho_{ij}$, a rate
$\mu_{ij}=s_i\rho_{ij}$, and a zero-inflation probability $\pi_{ij}\in[0,1]$, with
a gene-specific over-dispersion $\theta_j>0$:
$$
\mu_{ij}=s_i\,\rho_{ij},\qquad
p_{\mathrm{ZINB}}(x_{ij}\mid\pi_{ij},\mu_{ij},\theta_j)
=\pi_{ij}\,\delta_0(x_{ij})+(1-\pi_{ij})\,
\underbrace{\frac{\Gamma(x_{ij}+\theta_j)}{\Gamma(\theta_j)\,x_{ij}!}
\left(\frac{\theta_j}{\theta_j+\mu_{ij}}\right)^{\theta_j}
\left(\frac{\mu_{ij}}{\theta_j+\mu_{ij}}\right)^{x_{ij}}}_{p_{\mathrm{NB}}(x_{ij}\mid\mu_{ij},\theta_j)},
$$ {#eq-ch08-zinb}

where $\Gamma$ is the gamma function and $\delta_0$ is the point mass at zero; the
mixture in @eq-ch08-zinb is the model's account of technical dropout,
distinguishing "not captured" from "not expressed". The library size enters
through $\mu_{ij}=s_i\rho_{ij}$ and,
together with $\mathbf{b}_i$, is an explicit input to the decoder, which is what
makes the latent space depth- and batch-aware rather than depth- and
batch-dominated.

scVI assumes the genes are **conditionally independent given the latent**, so the
observation log-likelihood factors over genes:
$$
\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\mathbf{z}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)
=\sum_{j=1}^{g}\log p_{\mathrm{ZINB}}\!\big(x_{ij}\mid\pi_{ij},\mu_{ij},\theta_j\big).
$$ {#eq-ch08-scvi-likelihood}

The posterior $p_\theta(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)$ is
intractable, so scVI trains a variational autoencoder [@kingma2014auto] whose
encoder $q_\phi(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)$ maximizes the
**evidence lower bound** (ELBO) of the marginal likelihood
$p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)=\int p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\mathbf{z}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)\,p(\mathbf{z}_i)\,d\mathbf{z}_i$:
$$
\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;\mathbf{x}_i)
=\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)}
\!\big[\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\mathbf{z}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)\big]
-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)\,\lVert\,p(\mathbf{z}_i)\big).
$$ {#eq-ch08-elbo}

Both terms in @eq-ch08-elbo are computable: the first is the expected ZINB
likelihood of @eq-ch08-scvi-likelihood evaluated at a reparameterized sample
from $q_\phi$, and the second is a closed-form KL to the standard-normal prior
$p(\mathbf{z}_i)=\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\mathbf{I})$. The bound follows from
Jensen's inequality applied to the log of an expectation,
$$
\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)
=\log\!\int q_\phi(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\cdot)\,
\frac{p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\mathbf{z}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)\,p(\mathbf{z}_i)}
{q_\phi(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\cdot)}\,d\mathbf{z}_i
\;\ge\;\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;\mathbf{x}_i),
$$
with the gap equal to the posterior approximation error,
$$
\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)-\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;\mathbf{x}_i)
=D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(q_\phi(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)\,\lVert\,p_\theta(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\mathbf{x}_i,s_i,\mathbf{b}_i)\big)\;\ge\;0 .
$$ {#eq-ch08-elbo-gap}
@eq-ch08-elbo-gap identifies the ELBO as
$\log p_\theta(\mathbf{x}_i\mid\cdot)$ minus a nonnegative KL gap, so maximizing
$\mathcal{L}$ both raises the marginal likelihood and tightens the variational
approximation. The mean of $q_\phi(\mathbf{z}_i\mid\cdot)$ is taken as the cell
embedding.

Because the batch term is explicit in the decoder, the latent space is *designed*
to retain biology while the decoder absorbs batch-specific scale. scVI is
implemented in the `scvi-tools` library [@gayoso2022python]. The latent space is
reusable: the same $\mathbf{z}_i$ supports clustering, visualization, and
differential-expression testing under a count-appropriate noise model, and
benchmarks place scVI among the strongest integration methods
[@luecken2022benchmarking].

## scANVI and annotation transfer

scANVI [@xu2021probabilistic] extends scVI to semi-supervised settings: a subset
of cells carries cell-type labels, and a classifier head on the latent space
propagates those labels to unlabeled cells during training. The result is a
latent space that is both batch-corrected and class-discriminative, used for
reference-based annotation.

## totalVI and multimodal cells

totalVI [@gayoso2021joint] generalizes the same framework to CITE-seq data, where
each cell has both an RNA count vector and a surface-protein count vector. It
infers a *joint* latent space and two modality-specific likelihoods, so that RNA
and protein both inform a single embedding and one modality can help denoise the
other. Multimodal integration is the subject of Chapter 9.

## The standard latent-variable pipeline

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["Raw counts X and batch b"] --> B["Latent encoder q(z|x,b)"]
  B --> C["Latent embedding z"]
  C --> D["Decoder: ZINB likelihood p(x|z,b)"]
  D --> A
  C --> E["Downstream: clustering, annotation, DE"]
  C --> F["UMAP, visualization only"]
```

The figure makes explicit the structure shared by scVI, scANVI, and totalVI: a
count likelihood, a latent embedding, an explicit batch covariate in the
generative model, and a single low-dimensional space reused for many downstream
tasks. The key design decision — encoding batch in the *decoder* rather than
removing it from the input — is what lets the same latent space serve both
integration and biological discovery.

# Cell Foundation Models

A second wave models cells by analogy with language models: genes are tokens,
expression levels are values, and a transformer is pretrained on millions of
cells before being applied to new tasks.

## scBERT

scBERT [@yang2022scbert] tokenizes each cell as a ranked gene-expression
sequence and pretrains a BERT-style transformer with a masked-expression
objective, then fine-tunes for cell-type annotation. It demonstrated that
gene-level self-supervision transfers across datasets.

## Geneformer

Geneformer [@theodoris2023transfer] pretrains on a large corpus of single-cell
transcriptomes using **rank-value encoding** — each cell is a sequence of genes
ordered by expression rank — and shows transfer to dosage-sensitivity and
network-biology prediction tasks. Its design emphasizes transfer learning for
network biology rather than embedding quality as such.

## scGPT and scFoundation

scGPT [@cui2024scgpt] is a generative transformer pretrained across tens of
millions of cells, with a unified token scheme for genes and expression bins and
a fine-tuning recipe spanning annotation, perturbation prediction, and
multi-omic integration. scFoundation [@hao2024large] develops a large-scale
transcriptomic model with a read-depth-aware pretraining objective and a
"cell sentence" factorization, targeting downstream tasks directly from the
pretrained representation. Both are generative foundation models in the sense of
Chapter 13; both inherit the masked-token pretraining idea from language models.

## What foundation models add — and their caveats

These models promise a single pretrained representation reusable across tissues
and assays, reducing the need for task-specific training. A coarse comparison of
the four, by input encoding and pretraining objective:

| Model | Input encoding | Pretraining objective | Primary source |
|---|---|---|---|
| scBERT | Ranked gene sequence + expression bins | Masked gene-expression prediction | [@yang2022scbert] |
| Geneformer | Genes ranked by expression (rank-value) | Masked gene prediction | [@theodoris2023transfer] |
| scGPT | Gene tokens + expression-value bins | Masked modeling, generative | [@cui2024scgpt] |
| scFoundation | Gene tokens with read-depth modeling | Masked expression, depth-aware | [@hao2024large] |

The open questions are evaluation (see below), whether they beat well-tuned scVI on standard
integration benchmarks [@luecken2022benchmarking], and whether rank-based or
bin-based tokenization loses information that a count model preserves. The
honest summary is that cell foundation models are promising and widely used, but
the evidence that they dominate simpler probabilistic embeddings is uneven.

# Gene Embeddings and Transfer Across Datasets

Cells are not the only entities to embed. A **gene embedding** is a learned
$d$-dimensional vector per gene, obtained either as a row of a factorized
expression matrix or as an output of a gene-token encoder. Gene embeddings let
one reason about gene–gene similarity, co-expression modules, and, via
attention over gene tokens in scGPT [@cui2024scgpt] and scBERT
[@yang2022scbert], which genes drive a prediction.

Cross-dataset transfer is the practical payoff. Reference-based annotation
(scANVI [@xu2021probabilistic]), query-to-reference mapping, and label
propagation all rest on the assumption that the latent geometry is stable across
experiments. That assumption is exactly what integration metrics test. When it
holds, a model trained on a well-annotated atlas can label a new experiment with
no new labels, which is the single most consequential use of cell embeddings in
practice. When it fails — a new tissue, a new species, a perturbation not seen in
the reference — the failure is usually silent, because the model still returns
confident labels. Transfer should therefore be validated on held-out cell types,
not only on held-out cells.

# Evaluation: Integration Metrics and the UMAP Caveat

Integration is not a single scalar. The benchmarking study of Luecken et al.
[@luecken2022benchmarking] established that methods trade off **batch removal**
against **biological conservation**, and no method wins on both axes
simultaneously. Evaluation therefore uses complementary metrics.

| Metric | What it measures | Needs labels? | Primary source |
|---|---|---|---|
| kBET | Rejection rate of the null that batch composition in a cell's neighborhood matches global composition (batch mixing, local) | No | [@buttner2019test] |
| iLISI | Effective number of batches represented in a cell's neighborhood (batch mixing, local) | No | [@korsunsky2019fast] |
| cLISI | Effective number of cell types in a neighborhood (cell-type separation) | Yes | [@korsunsky2019fast] |
| ARI / NMI | Agreement of cluster labels with ground-truth cell types | Yes | [@luecken2022benchmarking] |
| Graph connectivity | Fraction of each cell type connected within the integrated graph | Yes | [@luecken2022benchmarking] |
| Silhouette (batch vs. label) | Separation along batch vs. biological axes | Partly | [@luecken2022benchmarking] |

kBET [@buttner2019test] and LISI/iLISI/cLISI [@korsunsky2019fast] were introduced
with the Harmony integration method and are now the de facto neighborhood-level
metrics; ARI, NMI, graph connectivity, and silhouette are label-based and enter
through the benchmarking framework.

::: {.callout-warning}
## UMAP is not a benchmark
UMAP [@mcinnes2018umap] and t-SNE [@vandermaaten2008visualizing] are
visualization tools that optimize local neighborhoods under a stochastic layout.
Their coordinates are not metric, they can create apparent clusters from
continuous data, and a "well-mixed" UMAP can hide residual batch structure that
neighbor-based metrics detect. Report integration quality with neighborhood and
label metrics, and use UMAP only to *illustrate* a result already supported
numerically. This mirrors the broader visualization caveats in Chapter 12.
:::

The practical recipe is: fit a latent model, compute kBET/iLISI/cLISI plus at
least one label-based metric, and compare against a no-integration baseline.
A method that improves mixing while collapsing biologically distinct cell types
has traded the wrong thing.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key Takeaways
- A cell embedding replaces a sparse, depth-dominated count vector with a
  low-dimensional representation whose geometry encodes biological similarity.
- Classical pipelines (normalize → HVG → PCA → kNN graph → UMAP) are fast
  baselines but are not batch-aware; probabilistic models fix this by putting the
  batch covariate inside a generative likelihood [@lopez2018deep].
- scVI, scANVI, and totalVI share one recipe — a count likelihood, a latent
  embedding, and an explicit batch term — differing in supervision and modality
  [@lopez2018deep; @xu2021probabilistic; @gayoso2021joint].
- Cell foundation models (scBERT, Geneformer, scGPT, scFoundation) pretrain on
  gene-token sequences and transfer across tasks, but their advantage over tuned
  probabilistic models is task-dependent and must be benchmarked
  [@yang2022scbert; @theodoris2023transfer; @cui2024scgpt; @hao2024large].
- Evaluate integration with neighborhood metrics (kBET, LISI) and label-based
  metrics (ARI, NMI, graph connectivity); never treat a UMAP as quantitative
  evidence [@buttner2019test; @korsunsky2019fast; @luecken2022benchmarking].
:::
